make-ten.why: Ten is the number our whole system is built on, so getting to a ten makes everything downstream easy. Splitting 8 + 5 into 8 + 2 + 3 is the single technique behind almost all mental arithmetic.
traps: You must split the *second* number by what the first one needs, not by half.

add-facts.why: Addition facts to 20 need to be recall, not calculation. Not because speed matters in itself, but because every later step — fractions, algebra, long division — spends working memory, and any spent on 7 + 8 is unavailable for the actual problem.
traps: If you count on fingers past about 12 you will drop one. Use making ten instead.

sub-facts.why: Subtraction is best read as a missing addend: 13 - 8 asks what adds to 8 to make 13. Counting up is faster, less error-prone, and it is exactly how a cashier gives change.
traps: Order matters: 8 - 13 is not 13 - 8. Subtraction is not commutative.

add-sub-relation.why: Addition and subtraction are one operation read in two directions. Seeing that lets you check any answer instantly and solve any missing-number problem without a new technique — which is also how you will later solve equations.
traps: In ~\square - 8 = 5~ the missing number is the biggest one, 13. Subtracting makes things smaller, so the unknown must have started larger.

mental-add-strategies.why: Mental arithmetic is not the written method done in your head — it is a different, better set of moves: round to a friendly number and compensate. 47 + 29 becomes 47 + 30 - 1.
traps: Compensate in the right direction. Adding 30 instead of 29 means you added one too many, so you take one back off.
